name: Jiangshi (僵尸 / 殭屍)
facts: A jiangshi is an undead or reanimated corpse in Chinese legends and folklore, often called a Chinese hopping vampire in English.

Hong Kong cinema fixed the popular image of a stiff corpse in Qing official dress that hops; folkloric accounts instead describe a more dangerous corpse that can run, and an old enough one, or one that has absorbed enough yang, that can fly.

J. J. M. de Groot linked the fear to unburied corpses and to qi animating exposed bodies. The nighttime trade of 'corpse-driving' — tying a body to bamboo so it could be carried home for burial — also produced the look of a hopping corpse.

sources.title: Jiangshi
sources.supports: Undead corpse; hop is a cinema image; folklore allows running and flight; corpse-driving practice.

parodyPotential: A tower corpse furious that films taught it to hop, when it would rather sprint the corridor.

name: Huli jing (狐狸精)
facts: Huli jing are Chinese fox spirits, usually able to shapeshift, and they may be benevolent or malevolent.
Names in the tradition sort them into fox immortal, fox god, fox saint, fox king, fox demon, fox clan, and nine-tailed fox (jiuweihu).
Whether a fox spirit is a good or bad omen depends on the story. The nine-tailed fox motif later passed into Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese tradition.

sources.title: Huli jing
sources.supports: Shapeshifting fox spirits, good or bad, including the nine-tailed fox and later transmission.

parodyPotential: A nine-resume fox who keeps one tail per failed job interview.

name: Nian (年獸)
facts: The nian is a beast said to live under the sea or in the mountains. The character nian more usually means year or new year.
The earliest written sources that treat the nian as a creature date to the early 20th century, so it is unclear whether it is ancient mythology or an oral tradition first written down then.
It is now a key Chinese New Year figure. Scholars cite it as the reason for practices such as wearing red and making noise with drums and fireworks.

sources.title: Nian
sources.supports: Sea or mountain beast; early-20th-century written sources; linked by scholars to red clothes and New Year noise.

parodyPotential: A New Year beast that files a noise complaint and then flees its own fireworks.

name: Pixiu (貔貅)
facts: The pixiu is a Chinese mythical hybrid, described as resembling a strong winged lion, and treated as a protector of the souls of the dead, of xian, and of feng shui practitioners.
It is an auspicious wealth creature whose appetite is said to be only for gold, silver, and jewels, drawing cai qi (wealth-energy) from all directions.
A two-antler form, the female Bixie, wards off evil; a one-antler form, the male Tianlu, seeks wealth. Statues are used to attract money.

sources.title: Pixiu
sources.supports: Winged-lion wealth guardian; gold appetite; Bixie and Tianlu antler types.

parodyPotential: A treasury beast that can swallow coins and cannot spit them back out.

name: Taotie (饕餮)
facts: The taotie is an ancient Chinese mythological creature, one of the Four Perils in classics such as the Classic of Mountains and Seas, with Hundun, Qiongqi, and Taowu.
It is the familiar frontal, symmetrical mask on Shang and Zhou ritual bronze vessels such as dings: raised eyes and typically no lower jaw.
Some scholars trace related designs to Neolithic jades, including the Liangzhu culture.

sources.title: Taotie
sources.supports: Four Perils member; bronze mask with eyes and usually no lower jaw.

parodyPotential: A mask-face boss with no chin who still tries to eat the loot pile.

name: Hundun (混沌)
facts: Hundun names both a legendary faceless being in Chinese mythology and the primordial central chaos of Chinese cosmogony, compared with the world egg.
The taotie article lists Hundun among the Four Perils beside Taotie, Qiongqi, and Taowu.

sources.title: Hundun
sources.supports: Faceless being and primordial chaos.

sources.title: Taotie
sources.supports: Hundun is named as one of the Four Perils.

parodyPotential: A faceless round boss who wins by having no features left to target.

name: Penghou (彭侯)
facts: The Penghou, literally 'drumbeat marquis', is a tree spirit. The Baize tu says a creature evolved from the essence of wood looks like a black dog with no tail, and that its meat can be eaten.
The Soushenji tells of Jing Shu felling a camphor tree in the Wu kingdom: the wood bled, and inside was an animal like a dog with a human face, which he identified as a Penghou and stewed.
Li Shizhen's Bencao gangmu repeats those sources. Toriyama Sekien later drew the Japanese reading Hōkō from the same Chinese texts.

sources.title: Penghou
sources.supports: Tailless black-dog tree spirit; camphor-tree story; later a Sekien yokai under the Japanese name.

parodyPotential: A camphor-tree dog with a human face who objects to being a recipe.

name: Bai Ze (白澤)
facts: Bai Ze is a mythical creature from ancient Chinese legend, later introduced to Japan under the same name in the Tang period.
The Book of Song tradition of the Bai Ze tu says this divine creature knows the world's ghosts and gods. The Yellow Emperor entrusted it to draw and annotate them.

Appearance differs by source: the Ming San Cai Tu Hui gives green hair, a dragon head, a horn, and flight; the History of Yuan gives a tiger head and red mane. Households hung Bai Ze drawings to ward off spirit harm.

sources.title: Bai Ze
sources.supports: All-knowing divine beast; ghost diagram for the Yellow Emperor; protective household images.

parodyPotential: A librarian of ghosts whose diagram is always one entry out of date. Do not mock the protective custom.

name: Zhenniao (鴆鳥)
facts: Zhenniao, often just zhen, literally 'poison-feather bird', is the name given in Chinese myths, annals, and poetry to poisonous birds once said to live in what is now southern China.
The fifth chapter of the Classic of Mountains and Seas describes the zhen as resembling an eagle and places it on several southern mountains, including Mount Nüji in Jiangsu.

sources.title: Zhenniao
sources.supports: Poison-feather bird resembling an eagle in southern mountains, from the Shanhaijing.

parodyPotential: A southern eagle whose feathers are a walking hazard label.

name: Xiangliu (相柳 / 相繇)
facts: Xiangliu, called Xiangyao in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, is a venomous nine-headed snake monster that brings floods and destruction.
The body may be shown coiled. Older woodcuts cluster the nine heads on one neck; many modern pictures give each head its own neck, like a hydra.

sources.title: Xiangliu
sources.supports: Venomous nine-headed flood snake; head arrangement varies by picture.

parodyPotential: A nine-headed flood snake that cannot agree which way the river should run.

name: Xiezhi (獬豸), also haechi
facts: The xiezhi is a mythical creature of Chinese origin across Sinospheric legends. It resembles an ox or goat, with thick dark fur, bright eyes, and one long horn.
It is said to understand human speech and to know right from wrong. Finding a corrupt official, it rams them with the horn and devours them. It is a symbol of justice.
The English Wikipedia disambiguation for Haechi points to the xiezhi as the legendary creature in Chinese and Korean mythology and as the Seoul mascot.

sources.title: Xiezhi
sources.supports: One-horned justice beast that gores corrupt officials.

sources.title: Haechi
sources.supports: Disambiguation identifies the xiezhi with Chinese and Korean mythology and the Seoul mascot.

parodyPotential: A one-horn auditor who headbutts only the player who cheated the loot roll. Avoid mocking the Seoul civic symbol.

name: Kui (夔)
facts: Kui is a polysemous name. Classic texts use it for a legendary musician who invented music and dancing, for a one-legged mountain demon or rain-god, and for the kuiniu wild yak or buffalo.
The one-legged Kui is variously said to resemble a Chinese dragon, a drum, or a monkey with a human face.

sources.title: Kui (Chinese mythology)
sources.supports: Musician, one-legged mountain demon or rain-god, and wild bovine share the name.

parodyPotential: A one-legged drum-demon who keeps perfect time and terrible balance. Do not target the rain-god sense.

name: Chinese dragon (long / loong, 龍)
facts: The Chinese dragon, long or loong, is a legendary creature in Chinese mythology, folklore, and culture at large.
It has many animal-like forms, including turtles and fish, but is most often shown as snake-like with four legs.

Scholars have offered four origin theories: snakes, Chinese alligators, thunder worship, and nature worship. Dragons traditionally symbolize potent auspicious power, especially control of water and weather.

sources.title: Chinese dragon
sources.supports: Snake-like four-legged auspicious weather and water being.

parodyPotential: Research record only for a sacred auspicious symbol. Prefer the hornless jiaolong if a comic flood-serpent is needed.

name: Qilin (麒麟)
facts: The qilin is a legendary hooved chimera in Chinese mythology, said to appear with the imminent arrival or passing of a sage or illustrious ruler.
It is a specific type within the lin family of one-horned beasts, and it also appears in other Chinese-influenced mythologies.

sources.title: Qilin
sources.supports: Hooved chimera and omen of a sage or ruler; one-horned lin type.

parodyPotential: An omen beast that arrives for a wise ruler and looks embarrassed when the party is not one.

name: Fenghuang (鳳凰)
facts: Fenghuang are mythological birds across the Sinosphere, understood to reign over all other birds.

Males and females were once called feng and huang separately. The gender split is usually dropped now, and the fenghuang is generally treated as feminine and paired with the traditionally masculine Chinese dragon.
Calling it a Chinese phoenix is a Western habit; similarities to the Persian or Western phoenix are superficial.

sources.title: Fenghuang
sources.supports: Bird-sovereign paired with the dragon; not a Western phoenix.

parodyPotential: A bird-sovereign who refuses to be called a phoenix on the nameplate.

name: Jiaolong (蛟龍)
facts: The jiaolong, or jiao, is a serpent-like dragon in Chinese mythology, often defined as a scaled dragon. Certain scholars say it is hornless, and it is described as aquatic or river-dwelling. It may once have referred to a crocodile.
Scholars point to non-Sinitic southern origins. Ancient texts say the Yue tattooed their bodies to ward these monsters off.
English translators render jiao as jiao-dragon, crocodile, flood dragon, scaly dragon, or even kraken.

sources.title: Jiaolong
sources.supports: Hornless aquatic scaled dragon; Yue tattoos as a ward.

parodyPotential: A hornless river dragon still annoyed that people got tattoos instead of paying the toll.

name: Chi (螭)
facts: Chi means either a hornless dragon or a mountain demon (chimei) in Chinese mythology.
Hornless dragons were a common motif in ancient Chinese art. The chiwen, or 'hornless-dragon mouth', was an imperial roof ornament.

sources.title: Chi (mythology)
sources.supports: Hornless dragon or mountain demon; chiwen roof ornament.

parodyPotential: A roof-ornament dragon that eats gutter water and files leak reports.

name: Bixi (贔屭)
facts: Bixi is a figure from Chinese mythology, one of the nine sons of the Dragon King, depicted as a dragon with a turtle's shell.
Stone bixi have served for centuries as plinths under commemorative steles, including in later imperial funerary complexes, and also under bridges and archways.
People traditionally rub the sculptures for luck, which damages them. They occur across East Asia and the Russian Far East.

sources.title: Bixi
sources.supports: Dragon-turtle son of the Dragon King, used as a stele plinth and rubbed for luck.

parodyPotential: A dragon-turtle who has been holding the same tablet up for centuries and would like a shift change.

name: Feilian (飛廉)
facts: Feilian is a Chinese wind spirit from a southern tradition, later identified with and absorbed under the main wind deity Fengbo.
The name has also been tied to a late Shang minister and to the mythical phoenix. After losing the rank of wind-master, Feilian kept a separate identity as a mythical creature.

sources.title: Feilian
sources.supports: Southern wind spirit later folded into Fengbo, surviving as a creature.

parodyPotential: A retired wind spirit who still gusts the discard pile when ignored.

name: Wangliang (魍魎)
facts: A wangliang is a malevolent spirit. Readings of the name include a wilderness spirit like the kui, a water spirit akin to the Chinese dragon, a fever demon like the three-legged poisonous turtle called yu, and a graveyard ghost also called wangxiang or fangliang.
One description is a man-eating demon like a three-year-old child, with brown skin, red eyes, long ears, and beautiful hair.

sources.title: Wangliang
sources.supports: Several malevolent-spirit readings, including a child-shaped man-eater.

parodyPotential: Use the wilderness or graveyard reading. Do not build a joke on the child-shaped man-eater.

name: Daji (妲己) as fox spirit
facts: Daji is the alleged favorite consort of Di Xin, last king of Shang. She is not recorded in contemporary oracle-bone inscriptions.

In later legend and fiction she is a malevolent fox spirit who kills and impersonates the real Daji. That fox identification is traced at least to the Tang, and it was spread by works such as Wu Wang fa Zhou pinghua, Fengshen yanyi, and Lieguo zhi.

She is a stock example of a beautiful femme fatale blamed for a dynasty's fall. In 1111 a Song edict ordered destruction of many Kaifeng spirit shrines, including shrines of Daji; suppression of fox cults was unsuccessful.

sources.title: Daji
sources.supports: Later fox-spirit impersonator of a Shang consort; shrine suppression in 1111; not on oracle bones.

parodyPotential: A fox who stole a queen's name and is still bad at paperwork. Do not treat the shrine cult as a punchline.

name: Bai Suzhen (白素貞), Lady White Snake
facts: Bai Suzhen, also Lady Bai, is a thousand-year-old white snake spirit and the title figure of the Legend of the White Snake, one of China's four great folktales.
The legend is a romance between the snake spirit and a man named Xu Xian. The story has changed by era and region and has been told in novels, operas, and other media.
In some versions Bai Suzhen becomes a goddess, and worshippers call her Madam White Snake. She is widely taken as a symbol of true love and kind-heartedness.

sources.title: Bai Suzhen
sources.supports: Thousand-year white snake of a great folktale; sometimes worshipped as Madam White Snake.

sources.title: Legend of the White Snake
sources.supports: Romance of Xu Xian and Bai Suzhen; one of the four great folktales.

parodyPotential: An affectionate tower echo of a devoted snake-doctor, not a mockery of Madam White Snake worship.

name: Mogwai (魔鬼), as a word
facts: Mogwai is the Cantonese reading of 魔鬼, meaning monster, evil spirit, devil, or demon. Mandarin reads the same characters móguǐ.
Mo comes from Sanskrit māra, evil beings, literally death. Examples given are the yecha (yaksha) and the luocha (rakshasa), both reaching Chinese lore through Buddhism.
This is a class word, not a single species, and it is not the creature from the 1984 film that borrowed the sound of the word.

sources.title: Mogwai (Chinese culture)
sources.supports: Cantonese word for demon; Sanskrit māra; yaksha and rakshasa as examples.

parodyPotential: Do not design a furry film-gremlin. The word is a generic demon label.

name: Oni (鬼)
facts: An oni is a yōkai, demon, or ogre in Japanese folklore, said to live in caves, deep mountains, or hell.

They are hugely strong, tied to thunder and lightning, and storied as murderous and cannibal. Typical pictures show horns, huge teeth, sometimes a third eye, red blue black or yellow skin, a tiger-skin loincloth, and an iron kanabō.

They can change shape to win trust. Heian setsuwa show them eating a person in one bite (onihitokuchi). They have also been linked to good fortune. Shuten-dōji is regarded as the most famous and strongest oni.

sources.title: Oni
sources.supports: Horned club-wielding ogre; shapeshifting; Heian man-eating tales; also a luck association.

parodyPotential: A horned hall monitor whose club is heavier than the joke.

name: Kappa (河童)
facts: The kappa, 'river-child', is a major Japanese water yōkai living in ponds and rivers, also called kawatarō in some places.
Older accounts make them drowners of people, horses, and cattle. Later tales have a captured kappa, sometimes with an arm pulled off, repay forgiveness with labor or a secret medicine.

They are pictured as green, slimy or scaly, webbed, and turtle-shelled. A dish (sara) of water on the head is their strength; spill it and they weaken. They like cucumbers and sumo, and are accused of pulling out a mythical organ called the shirikodama.

sources.title: Kappa (folklore)
sources.supports: River monster; head-dish; cucumbers; sumo; shift from killer to indebted helper.

parodyPotential: A river auditor who will wrestle for a cucumber and folds if anyone bows low enough to spill the dish.

name: Tengu (天狗)
facts: Tengu, 'heavenly dog', are legendary creatures in Shinto belief, classed as yōkai or as kami.

They were first thought of as birds of prey and were tied to a monkey deity, drawn with human, monkey, and bird traits. Sarutahiko Ōkami is considered the model of the red-faced long-nosed konoha-tengu now treated as the popular tengu.
Buddhism long called them disruptive demons and omens of war. The image softened into dangerous but protective mountain and forest spirits, associated with Shugendō and usually dressed as yamabushi.

sources.title: Tengu
sources.supports: Heavenly-dog yokai or kami; long-nosed yamabushi form; Sarutahiko as model of the konoha-tengu.

parodyPotential: A long-nosed mountain guide who gives terrible directions on purpose. Do not parody Sarutahiko Ōkami.

name: Kitsune (狐)
facts: In popular Japanese folklore the kitsune is a fox or fox spirit with the supernatural ability to shapeshift or bewitch other living beings.

The bake-danuki article says that in some regions tanuki are reputed to share kitsune-like powers of shapeshifting and possession. The noppera-bō article lists kitsune among shapeshifters who may stage a faceless scare.

sources.title: Kitsune
sources.supports: Fox spirit that shapeshifts or bewitches.

sources.title: Bake-danuki
sources.supports: Some regions credit tanuki with kitsune-like shapeshifting and possession.

parodyPotential: A fox clerk who files the party under the wrong names. Do not attach this record to Inari worship; that link was not in the sources read.

name: Bake-danuki (化け狸)
facts: Bake-danuki are yōkai in classics and local legends, associated with the Japanese raccoon dog, the tanuki. The literary bake-danuki is a strange or supernatural animal, not just the real mammal.
In some regions they are said to shapeshift or possess people, abilities also attributed to kitsune.
Named tanuki of Sado, Awa, and Kagawa, among others, became subjects of ritual.

sources.title: Bake-danuki
sources.supports: Supernatural tanuki; shapeshift and possess; some named ones receive rites.

parodyPotential: A raccoon-dog merchant whose leaf disguise is a bad receipt. Leave the ritually named tanuki alone.

name: Yuki-onna (雪女)
facts: Yuki-onna, 'snow woman', is a yūrei or yōkai in Japanese folklore, also common in literature, film, and animation.
Regional names include yuki-musume, yukihime, yuki-onago, yukijorō, yuki-onba, yukinba in Ehime, and yukifuri-baba in Nagano, plus icicle names such as tsurara-onna.
The English lead read for this project lists names and does not specify powers. Do not treat ice-breath or a spare-the-youth bargain as sourced from this pass.

sources.title: Yuki-onna
sources.supports: Snow-woman yurei or yokai under many regional names; powers not in the lead.

parodyPotential: A snow woman whose only confirmed trait here is that every village files her under a different name.

name: Noppera-bō (のっぺらぼう)
facts: The noppera-bō is a faceless yōkai that looks human but has no face. An 18th-century version calls a similar being a nupperibō.
Lafcadio Hearn's 1904 story 'Mujina', set in Edo, uses the double scare: a man flees a blank-faced woman and tells a soba-shop keeper, who then turns around blank-faced.
The blank face is sometimes said to be a trick by a mujina, kitsune, or tanuki.

sources.title: Noppera-bō
sources.supports: Faceless human yokai; Hearn's soba-shop double scare; sometimes a beast's trick.

parodyPotential: A help-desk ghost whose face loads only after you stop asking.

name: Rokurokubi (ろくろ首)
facts: Rokurokubi are yōkai who look almost human. One type stretches its neck; another, the nukekubi, detaches its head and lets it fly.
They appear in classical kaidan and in yōkai picture-books. The krasue article notes them as a Japanese comparison for Southeast Asian flying-head spirits, not as the same being.

sources.title: Rokurokubi
sources.supports: Stretching neck or detachable flying head.

sources.title: Krasue
sources.supports: Names nukekubi and rokurokubi as a Japanese comparison, not an identity.

parodyPotential: A customer whose neck reaches the back of the shop while the body stays in line.

name: Nurikabe (塗壁)
facts: The nurikabe, 'plastered wall', is a yōkai said to appear as an invisible wall that blocks or misdirects night travelers. It is described as too tall to climb and too wide to walk around.
Kunio Yanagita recorded an early prominent example. A 17th-century scroll at Brigham Young University, noticed in 2007, labels a white dog-elephant-like creature as nurikabe.
Shigeru Mizuki's manga nurikabe was inspired by his own claim of being stuck in coal tar in New Guinea. That character is a modern depiction, not the folklore wall.

sources.title: Nurikabe
sources.supports: Invisible night wall; Yanagita; 17th-century dog-elephant picture; Mizuki's version is separate.

parodyPotential: An invisible wall that is simply the next room refusing to load.

name: Tsukumogami (付喪神)
facts: Tsukumogami, literally 'tool kami', are tools that have acquired a spirit. One theory in a commentary on The Tales of Ise, traced to the Onmyōki, counts hundred-year-old shapeshifted foxes and tanuki as tsukumogami too.
The characters 九十九神, 'ninety-nine kami', are a modern spelling that stresses age.

Komatsu Kazuhiko argues the tool-yōkai idea spread in the middle ages and later faded, and that Bakumatsu prints revived a picture without the old belief. The popular 'any object turns alive at 100' rule is widespread and disputed.

sources.title: Tsukumogami
sources.supports: Tools that gain a kami; the 100-year rule is a modern and contested reading.

parodyPotential: A union of retired tools. Do not treat the hundred-year rule as settled folklore.

name: Kasa-obake (傘おばけ)
facts: Kasa-obake are umbrella ghosts or yōkai. They are sometimes, not always, classed as tsukumogami that old umbrellas become.
Other names include karakasa-obake, kasa-bake, and karakasa kozō.
The English lead read here does not describe a single eye, a single leg, or a licking tongue. Those details are not sourced in this pass.

sources.title: Kasa-obake
sources.supports: Umbrella yokai, sometimes a tsukumogami; one-eye one-leg look not in the lead.

parodyPotential: An umbrella that opens indoors on purpose. Do not add a one-eyed foot unless a later source is fetched.

name: Umibōzu (海坊主)
facts: Umibōzu, 'sea monk', is a yōkai in the form of a giant black human-like being.
It appears to sailors on calm seas that then turn rough. It breaks the ship as it rises, or it demands a ladle and drowns the crew.
The told escape is to hand it a bottomless ladle and sail while it is confused. Near-synonyms include umihōshi and uminyūdō.

sources.title: Umibōzu
sources.supports: Giant black sea figure; ladle demand; bottomless ladle as the escape.

parodyPotential: A sea monk who loses the fight to a ladle with no bottom.

name: Jorōgumo (絡新婦)
facts: Jorōgumo is a yōkai. The kanji 女郎蜘蛛 mean 'woman-spider'; the kanji usually written, 絡新婦, mean 'entangling newlywed woman' and are read with a jukujikun.
In Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō it is a spider woman manipulating small fire-breathing spiders.
The same word, in katakana, is the entomologists' name for the spider Trichonephila clavata, the joro spider. That animal is not the yōkai.

sources.title: Jorōgumo
sources.supports: Spider woman in Sekien, with small fire-breathing spiders; distinct from the joro spider species.

parodyPotential: A bridal spider who sends smaller spiders to do the talking. Do not draw the real joro spider as if it were the monster.

name: Amabie (アマビエ)
facts: Amabie is a legendary Japanese merfolk figure with a beak-like mouth and three legs or tail-fins. It is said to rise from the sea, prophesy a rich harvest or an epidemic, and tell people to copy its picture as a defense against illness.
It appears to be a variant or misspelling of amabiko or amahiko, a prophetic beast drawn with three or four legs and ape-like, daruma-like, bird-like, or fish-like features.
The known amabie picture is a woodblock dated 1846 at Kyoto University Library. An amabiko leaflet dated 1844 is older. These prints are yogenjū, prophecy-beasts.

sources.title: Amabie
sources.supports: Three-legged prophetic merfolk; copying the picture wards illness; 1846 print.

parodyPotential: A three-legged forecast fish that is only defeated by fan art.

name: Kamaitachi (鎌鼬)
facts: Kamaitachi is a yōkai from the oral tradition of the Kōshin'etsu region, and the name also covers the strange events it causes.
They ride dust devils and cut people with sickle-like front claws, leaving sharp wounds that do not hurt.
The name joins kama, sickle, and itachi, weasel.

sources.title: Kamaitachi
sources.supports: Sickle-weasel on a dust devil; painless cuts.

parodyPotential: A dust-devil weasel that deals papercuts and apologizes.

name: Akaname (垢嘗)
facts: The akaname, 'scum-licker' or 'filth-licker', is a yōkai drawn in Toriyama Sekien's 1776 Gazu Hyakki Yagyō. A precursor, akaneburi, is documented in 1686.
These beings are presumed to lick the filth that collects in bathtubs and bathrooms.

sources.title: Akaname
sources.supports: Sekien filth-licker of baths; 1776, with a 1686 precursor.

parodyPotential: A bathroom critic who rates grime and will not fight a clean tub.

name: Baku (獏)
facts: Baku are Japanese supernatural beings said to devour nightmares. They originate from the Chinese mo.
Legend says they were made from the spare pieces left when the gods finished the other animals.
The word baku now also means the Malayan tapir, and recent art has changed how the dream-eater is drawn. Dream-eating is the folkloric sense; the tapir is the modern animal sense.

sources.title: Baku (mythology)
sources.supports: Nightmare-eater made of leftover parts; Chinese mo origin; later confused with the tapir.

parodyPotential: A leftover-parts beast that eats the party's bad draws and sometimes a good one.

name: Raijū (雷獣)
facts: The raijū, 'thunder beast', is a yōkai associated with lightning, thunder, and the god Raijin. It is said to appear with lightning strikes.
Legends are centered in eastern Japan, and the name is common in Edo essays and modern folklore notes.
One theory says the nue shot by Minamoto no Yorimasa in the Heike was actually a raijū.

sources.title: Raijū
sources.supports: Thunder beast accompanying lightning and Raijin; a theory equates one nue with a raiju.

parodyPotential: A storm weasel that arrives only when the thunder cue fires. Do not parody Raijin.

name: Nue (鵺)
facts: The nue is a legendary yōkai or mononoke. In the Tale of the Heike it is a chimera with a monkey's head, a tiger's limbs, a tanuki's body, and a snake's front half for a tail. The Genpei jōsuiki instead gives a tiger's back, tanuki limbs, a fox tail, a cat's head, and a chicken's torso.
It is said to cry an eerie 'hyoo hyoo' like a scaly thrush, to be nocturnal, and to shapeshift, often into a flying black cloud.

In the Heike telling, a black cloud and the cry sicken an emperor until Minamoto no Yorimasa shoots the cloud and Ino Hayata finishes the creature. Kyoto, fearing a curse, floats the corpse downstream; mounds called Nuezuka mark burials, and disturbing one is said to have revived the grudge.

sources.title: Nue
sources.supports: Heike chimera; thrush cry; black-cloud form; Yorimasa's shot; cursed burial mounds.

parodyPotential: A mixed-up beast whose own bestiaries disagree about the parts.

name: Shuten-dōji (酒呑童子)
facts: Shuten-dōji is a mythical oni leader, killed in legend by Minamoto no Raikō (Yorimitsu).
After the beheading, the detached head still bit at the hero, who survived by wearing several helmets stacked on his head.
The lair is Mount Ōe northwest of Kyoto, or Mount Ibuki, depending on the version. Another theory places the original mountain at the western edge of Kyoto.

sources.title: Shuten-dōji
sources.supports: Oni leader; the severed head still bites; stacked helmets; Mount Oe lair.

parodyPotential: A drinking-oni whose defeat animation is a head that still tries one bite, answered by a stack of pots.

name: Gashadokuro (がしゃどくろ)
facts: Gashadokuro, literally 'rattling skeleton', also called odokuro, are mythical creatures the English Wikipedia places in modern Japanese mythology.
They are said to pick up people they wish to eat.
The lead read for this pass does not give a size, a starvation origin, or a ringing in the ears. Those details are not sourced here.

sources.title: Gashadokuro
sources.supports: Modern-mythology rattling skeleton that picks up people to eat; further traits not in the lead.

parodyPotential: A rattling skeleton that grabs one hero for a snack. Keep it distinct from older bone-ghosts; the article calls the tradition modern.

name: Nuppeppō (ぬっぺっぽう)
facts: The nuppeppō appears in Edo-period yōkai picture scrolls, including Gazu Hyakki Yagyō and Hyakkai zukan.
It is drawn as a blob of meat whose face and body are the same mass of wrinkles, so the features cannot be told apart.

sources.title: Nuppeppō
sources.supports: Edo picture-scroll blob of wrinkled meat with no separate face.

parodyPotential: A walking meatball with no face to aim at and no interest in being cooked.

name: Azukiarai (小豆洗い)
facts: Azukiarai, or azukitogi, is a ghostly sound like azuki beans being washed or ground, usually near a river.
Sometimes the spirit sings that it might grind beans or catch a person to eat, and anyone who approaches falls into the water.

It is seldom seen. When described, it is a short grotesque man with a large balding head, crooked teeth, a thin moustache, bulging yellow eyes, and ragged clothes, bent over a pail. The sound is sometimes blamed on a tanuki or a weasel.

sources.title: Azukiarai
sources.supports: Bean-washing sound by water; a song; approaching means falling in; sometimes a tanuki or weasel.

parodyPotential: A bean-washer whose chorus is the tell that the riverbank is a trap.

name: Wanyūdō (輪入道)
facts: Wanyūdō, literally 'wheel monk', also called Firewheel or Soultaker, is a yōkai in Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku gazu zoku hyakki.
The earliest reports are said to date to the Heian period.
The lead gives the names and the Sekien depiction. It does not describe the method of taking souls. Do not invent that method from the alias alone.

sources.title: Wanyūdō
sources.supports: Wheel-monk yokai in Sekien; Heian reports; aliases Firewheel and Soultaker.

parodyPotential: A flaming cartwheel monk who demands the right of way. Do not add a soul-stealing procedure that this source does not give.

name: Namazu (鯰)
facts: Namazu, or ōnamazu, is a giant underground catfish that causes earthquakes.
It lives under the Japanese islands and is guarded by the god Takemikazuchi at Kashima, who holds it down with a stone.
When that god's guard slips, the catfish thrashes and the earthquake follows.

sources.title: Namazu
sources.supports: Earthquake catfish pinned by the Kashima god's stone.

parodyPotential: A catfish under the tower whose thrash is the quake. Do not parody Takemikazuchi.

name: Bake-kujira (化鯨)
facts: Bake-kujira, 'ghost whale', also hone-kujira, 'bone whale', is a yōkai usually drawn as a whale's skeleton appearing at sea on stormy nights.
It is most closely tied to the coasts of western Japan, especially the Shimane peninsula.
It is generally read as a vengeful spirit of a whale, carrying resentment toward people involved in whaling.

sources.title: Bake-kujira
sources.supports: Skeletal whale on stormy nights; Shimane; grudge against whalers.

parodyPotential: A bone whale that arrives with the weather and will not beach for a selfie.

name: Futakuchi-onna (二口女)
facts: Futakuchi-onna, 'two-mouthed woman', is a yōkai with a normal mouth and a second mouth on the back of the head, under the hair, where the skull splits into lips, teeth, and a tongue.
The article places her with rokurokubi, kuchisake-onna, and yamauba: women transformed by a curse or supernatural disease, whose nature stays hidden until the end.

sources.title: Futakuchi-onna
sources.supports: Second mouth on the back of the head; hidden until revealed.

parodyPotential: A diner whose back-of-head mouth clears the plate the front mouth refused. Kuchisake-onna is a separate urban legend and is left to that research lane.

name: Tesso (鉄鼠)
facts: Tesso, 'iron rat', is a yōkai tied to the vengeful spirit of the Heian monk Raigō and to a mouse.
Toriyama Sekien gave it the name tesso in Gazu Hyakki Yagyō. Older names include Raigō-nezumi, from a Heike yomihon, and Mii-dera-nezumi, from Miidera in Ōtsu.

sources.title: Tesso
sources.supports: Vengeful monk as a rat; Sekien's name; also Raigo-nezumi and Miidera-nezumi.

parodyPotential: A monastery grudge that shows up as one iron rat and then as too many rats.

name: Zashiki-warashi (座敷童子)
facts: Zashiki-warashi, 'parlor child', are spirit-like beings told of mostly in Iwate. They are yōkai said to live in parlors or storerooms and to play pranks.

Seeing one is believed to bring good fortune, and families they dwell with are said to prosper. Yanagita's Tōno monogatari records them; chapter 17 says families with whom this spirit dwells become prosperous.

sources.title: Zashiki-warashi
sources.supports: Iwate parlor-child; pranks; the house prospers while they stay.

parodyPotential: A parlor child who pranks the hideout and whose leaving is the real disaster. Not a corpse-spirit.

name: Yamata no Orochi (八岐大蛇)
facts: Yamata no Orochi is a legendary eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent in the Kojiki and the Nihon shoki. The kami Susanoo defeats it to rescue Kushinadahime, and the Kusanagi sword, part of the imperial regalia, is found in a tail.
A local tradition says the serpent survived, fled to Mount Ibuki, and was venerated as Ibuki Daimyōjin.
Emperor Antoku and the dragon girl Longnü have been identified as incarnations of the serpent.

sources.title: Yamata no Orochi
sources.supports: Eight-headed serpent of the Kojiki; sword in the tail; venerated at Ibuki in one tradition.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. The serpent is tied to imperial-regalia myth and, locally, to veneration as Ibuki Daimyōjin.

name: Onryō (怨霊)
facts: Onryō, 'vengeful spirits', are yūrei believed able to harm the living, kill enemies, or cause disasters to redress wrongs suffered while alive.
They are often pictured as wronged women. Emperor Sutoku, Taira no Masakado, and Sugawara no Michizane are called the Three Great Onryō and were later enshrined as kami to calm them.

Masakado's head mound near Tokyo Station is still maintained; moves proposed for redevelopment were followed, in the telling, by worker deaths and accidents, so the mound stayed. Goryō are onryō of nobles who died unjust political deaths and became objects of reverence.

sources.title: Onryō
sources.supports: Vengeful ghosts; three great onryo deified; Masakado's mound still tended.

parodyPotential: A generic grudge-ghost may be usable. Do not parody Masakado's mound, Tenjin, or Sutoku.

name: Shisa (シーサー)
facts: Shisa are traditional Ryukyuan ornaments derived from Chinese guardian lions, usually in pairs, like a cross between a lion and a dog.
They are wards against some evils, placed on rooftops or beside house gates. The left figure traditionally has a closed mouth and the right an open mouth.
The open mouth wards off evil spirits; the closed mouth keeps good spirits in.

sources.title: Shisa
sources.supports: Okinawan lion-dog pairs; open mouth expels evil, closed mouth keeps good.

parodyPotential: A gate pair who argue about whether the door should stay open. Do not mock them as fake charms.

name: Komainu (狛犬)
facts: Komainu, often called lion-dogs in English, are pairs of lion-like statues that guard the gate of a Shinto shrine or stand before or inside the honden.

sources.title: Komainu
sources.supports: Lion-dog statue pairs guarding Shinto shrine gates or the inner sanctuary.

parodyPotential: Research record for a shrine guardian. Do not use it as a comedy enemy of the sanctuary.

name: Chinese guardian lions (石獅)
facts: Chinese guardian lions, or shishi, are traditional architectural ornaments, usually stone, also called stone lions and, in colloquial English, lion dogs, foo dogs, or fu dogs.
The form became popular in Chinese Buddhism. A pair, often a male with a ball and a female with a cub, was thought to protect a building from harmful spiritual influences and dangerous people.
From imperial palaces and tombs the lions spread across Asia, including Japan (komainu), Okinawa, Korea, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, among other places.

sources.title: Chinese guardian lions
sources.supports: Buddhist stone-lion pairs as building protectors; spread includes komainu and much of East and Southeast Asia.

parodyPotential: A threshold pair, male with a ball and female with a cub. 'Foo dog' is an English nickname, not a separate species, and not a film character.

name: Dokkaebi (도깨비)
facts: Dokkaebi are legendary creatures of Korean mythology and folklore, also called Korean ogres in English.
The same article calls them nature deities or spirits. They use extraordinary powers on humans, sometimes tricking them and sometimes helping them.
Legends give them many forms, 'a thousand faces', and they often wear hanbok.

sources.title: Dokkaebi
sources.supports: Trickster nature spirits or deities; many forms; often in hanbok.

parodyPotential: A hanbok trickster who wants a game, not a shrine gag. The source uses the word deities, so keep worship out of the joke.

name: Gumiho (구미호)
facts: Gumiho or kumiho, literally nine-tailed fox, is a creature in East Asian folktales and Korean legend, likened to the Chinese jiuweihu, the Japanese kitsune, and the Vietnamese hồ ly tinh.

The word first pointed to a magical fox in Joseon novels, or was a political insult for treacherous officials. Modern Korean usage widened it to fox spirits in traditional sources generally, which the article calls a conflation. Other names include bulyeou, baegyeou, maegu, and hogwi.

Korean myth usually paints foxes as deceptive, malevolent, and tragic, with rare benevolent or mountain-deity cases. Ancient records describe white fur and human transformation; nine tails show up in Korean historical records from Goryeo onward, not in the earliest kingdom records. Joseon novels also give some foxes a magical marble and more than one tail. The wish to become human is much more common in modern retellings than in older tales.

sources.title: Gumiho
sources.supports: Nine-tailed-fox name; Joseon literary history; deceptive fox; nine tails from Goryeo; marble in novels; becoming-human motif is mostly modern.

parodyPotential: A fox whose tail count is a Joseon novel device, not a power meter copied from a drama. Liver-eating was not the general trait in the sections read.

name: Bulgasari (불가살이)
facts: The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture defines the folklore bulgasari as an animal of tales that lives by eating iron and is a monster that cannot be killed. The name bulgasari (不可殺) means that.

In Korean tales its shape is not fixed: pig, ant, mouse, horse, insect, and others. It grows by eating metal and is destroyed by fire, its opposite in five-phase thought. Another name, hwagasal (火可殺), means it can be killed by fire.

Tales are usually set in the troubled years of Goryeo and Joseon, and historical figures appear. A common plot has persecuted people, often monks, make a small figure that eats iron and swells. The Joseon book Songnam japji reports a popular story of a Songdo monster that ate nearly all the iron and could not be killed. The encyclopedia separates this Korean tradition from the Chinese mo, which also eats metal. The 1962 and 1985 films are modern adaptations, not the shape of the tale.

sources.title: 불가사리, Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Academy of Korean Studies)
sources.supports: Iron-eating, unkillable-by-weapons tale creature; variable animal forms; fire as the counter; Songnam japji; not the Chinese mo and not the films.

parodyPotential: A scrap-eating creature whose silhouette changes every telling. Do not copy either film's monster suit. The Korean word also means starfish; that is a different encyclopedia entry.

name: Bulgae (불개)
facts: Bulgae or pulgae, 'fire dog', are mythical fire dogs in Korean mythology.
They come from the kingdom of darkness and chase the sun and the moon. Eclipses happen when they bite those bodies.

The article calls them strong, fierce, or hairy dogs, and says they are likely the Korean Sapsali, whose name means ghost-chasing dog. The breed link is the article's suggestion, not a separate source read here.

sources.title: Bulgae
sources.supports: Fire dogs from the dark kingdom; their bite on sun or moon is the eclipse.

parodyPotential: A kennel of fire dogs who bite the moon and then have to be called off.

name: Inmyeonjo (인면조)
facts: Inmyeonjo, 'human-face bird', is a Korean mythological bird with a human face, usually a woman's, sometimes a man's.

It is called a sacred bird linking sky and land, and it appears in Three Kingdoms tomb murals. Goguryeo examples include the Anak tombs, Dukheung-ri, Samsilchong, and Mooyongchong. At Dukheung-ri a pair named Cheonchu and Mansei are a longevity symbol, said to live a thousand years.
Silla gilt-bronze shoes and the Baekje gilt-bronze incense burner also show them. Some viewers instead identify a winged figure with the Buddhist kalavinka.

sources.title: Inmyeonjo
sources.supports: Human-faced sacred bird of tomb art; longevity symbol; sometimes read as a kalavinka.

parodyPotential: A thousand-year choir bird. Tomb murals and the kalavinka reading are not comedy targets.

name: Jeoseung Saja (저승사자)
facts: Jeoseung Saja, 'netherworld emissary', or Jeoseung Chasa, are psychopomps who guide the dead to the afterlife.
Like Yeomna, the king of the underworld, they are Buddhist divinities adopted into Korean shamanism and then tied to Korean beliefs that are not in Buddhism.

They are pictured as stern bureaucrats in Yeomna's service. Gangnim Doryeong carries the jeokpaeji, a red-cloth list of the dead, and calls a name three times so the soul must follow. Shamanic tradition often shows them as soldiers. The black durumagi, gat, and pale face popular today come from the KBS drama Hometown of Legends, not from the older picture.

sources.title: Jeoseung Saja
sources.supports: Buddhist-shamanic psychopomp; red name-list; the modern black-coat look is from a TV drama.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. These are Buddhist divinities still carried in shamanic tradition. The television costume is a separate copyrighted look.

name: Three-legged crow (Jinwu / Yangwu)
facts: The three-legged crow is a mythological creature in East Asian myth and art, believed to live in and represent the sun.
The most popular Chinese telling is the Yangwu or Jinwu, the golden crow.
The English lead read here does not use the Korean name samjok-o. That name is not claimed from this page.

sources.title: Three-legged crow
sources.supports: Sun-dwelling, sun-representing bird; Chinese golden crow Jinwu or Yangwu.

parodyPotential: Do not parody the sun crow. It is a sacred solar symbol, not a mascot.

name: Krasue (กระสือ)
facts: The krasue is a nocturnal female spirit of Southeast Asian folklore: a floating woman's head, usually young and beautiful, with internal organs still hanging from the neck.

Thai ethnographer Phraya Anuman Rajadhon says she is accompanied by a will-o'-the-wisp glow. She is often said to live in the same areas as the male spirit Krahang. She hovers because she has no lower body. The organs usually include the heart, the stomach, and a length of intestine.

The English article groups her with Khmer ahp, Lao kasu, Malay penanggalan, Balinese leyak, Vietnamese ma lai, and Philippine manananggal as related but regionally named traditions. Fangs and extra organs in films are contemporary pictures, not the older description.

sources.title: Krasue
sources.supports: Floating head with heart, stomach, and intestine; Anuman's glow; shares ground with Krahang; film fangs are modern.

parodyPotential: A floating head late for dinner because her own lights tangled. Living rural belief: joke the logistics, not the believers. Not the same card as penanggalan, ahp, or manananggal.

name: Krahang (กระหัง)
facts: Krahang is a male spirit of Thai folklore. He appears as a shirtless man in a traditional loincloth and flies at night.
He flies with two large kradong, round rice-winnowing baskets, in rural Thailand, and he often rides a sak tam khao, the long wooden pestle of a manual rice pounder.
The krasue article says the krasue is often said to live in the same areas.

sources.title: Krahang
sources.supports: Shirtless night flier using two winnowing baskets and often a rice pestle.

sources.title: Krasue
sources.supports: Krasue and Krahang are often said to share the same areas.

parodyPotential: A night flier whose mount is kitchen equipment.

name: Phi Kong Koi (ผีกองกอย)
facts: Phi Kong Koi is a Lao and Thai jungle ghost, often described as a one-legged phantom that hops and shouts 'Koi, koi, koi'.

Some people give it a fly-like tube mouth; others say it looks like a monkey or langur. Accounts agree it is ugly and, unusually, cannot climb trees. It is believed to suck blood from the toes of a traveler sleeping in the jungle. Crossing or keeping the feet together is the protection named on the English page.

Phya Anuman Rajadhon's 1954 essay The Phi, in the Journal of the Siam Society, describes the same one-legged hopper, the kong-koi cry, blood sucked from a sleeping wayfarer's toe, and says a loud shout frightens it off.

sources.title: Kong koi
sources.supports: One-legged hopping jungle ghost; koi cry; toe blood; crossed feet as protection.

sources.title: Phya Anuman Rajadhon, The Phi (Journal of the Siam Society, 1954 PDF)
sources.supports: One leg, the cry, toe blood, and retreat when shouted at.

parodyPotential: A one-legged jungle pest who loses if the party crosses its ankles and shouts. A dictionary note linking the name to an ethnic label is not used.

name: Mae Nak Phra Khanong (แม่นากพระโขนง)
facts: Mae Nak, or Nang Nak, is a well-known Thai ghost. Local folklore sets the story in the reign of King Rama IV. Wikipedia's creature summary calls her a legendary creature and a tutelary deity.

In the common legend, Nak of Phra Khanong Canal dies in childbirth while her husband Mak is away at war. He comes home to a wife and child who are already dead. She drops a lime while making nam phrik and stretches an arm to an impossible length to pick it up. Mak hides behind Blumea leaves, which ghosts are said to fear, and reaches Wat Mahabut, which she cannot enter. Later tellings have a monk confine her in a jar, or in the bone of her forehead.

A shrine at Wat Mahabut, moved in 1997 within the Suan Luang area, still receives offerings, especially from women asking for an easy birth or for a husband to avoid conscription. Historian Anek Nawikamul found an 1899 Siam Prabheth article by K.S.R. Kulap claiming a son invented the ghost to stop his father remarrying. That claim is a historical theory, not a replacement for the legend people tell.

sources.title: Mae Nak Phra Khanong
sources.supports: Childbirth death, the long arm and the lime, Blumea and the temple, a living shrine, and the 1899 skeptical article.

parodyPotential: If used at all, only as affection: a ghost who stretches for a dropped lime and will not start the raid until everyone has eaten. Do not mock the shrine, the childbirth death, or the people who ask her for help.

name: Nang Tani (นางตานี)
facts: Nang Tani, 'Lady of Tani', is a female spirit who haunts wild banana trees, Musa acuminata, called kluai tani.
She belongs to the tree maidens generically called Nang Mai, 'Lady of the Wood'. Similar spirits are noted in Cambodian and Lao tradition.
Other names are Phi Tani and Phrai Tani.

sources.title: Nang Tani
sources.supports: Young woman haunting wild banana trees; a kind of nang mai.

parodyPotential: A banana-tree lady who is offended by litter, not by the party existing.

name: Nang Ta-khian (นางตะเคียน)
facts: Nang Ta-khian, 'Lady of Ta-khian', is a female spirit of Thai folklore. She manifests as a woman who haunts Hopea odorata trees, called ta-khian in Thai.

sources.title: Nang Ta-khian
sources.supports: Woman who haunts Hopea odorata, the takhian tree.

parodyPotential: A great-tree lady. The English lead does not include dresses, lottery numbers, or curses; those are not claimed here.

name: Phi Phong (ผีโพง)
facts: Phi Phong, called Phi Pao in the northeast, is a northern Thai ghost said to come from black magic the practitioner could not control.

The belief ties the change to raising a herb called wan phi phong: white leaves, a fiery taste, a glow like a luminous woodlouse. As it matures, the leaves are said to take the shape of the grower's face, and the grower becomes Phi Phong.

By day they look ordinary. By night a soft flame shows in the nose and a resin like torch wax drips. Like krasue, krahang, and phi pop, they feed on filth: frogs, dung, rotting corpses, and afterbirth. They avoid people unless provoked, and then may throw objects. The article names a widow's bamboo carrying pole among the things thrown.

sources.title: Phong (ghost)
sources.supports: Failed northern sorcery; glowing herb; nose-flame; filth diet; usually flees people.

parodyPotential: A neighbor who is ordinary until the nose lights up. Do not play the afterbirth diet for laughs.

name: Phi Pop (ปอบ)
facts: Pop or Pob is a cannibalistic spirit of Thai folklore that devours human viscera. The English page says it is related to the Phi Fa spirit, without describing Phi Fa.

Katarzyna Ancuta, in eTropic 16.1 (2017), treats phi pop and phi krasue as beings with an appetite for viscera and for bodily discharges, perceived by many in Thailand as part of the natural world rather than as fiction. She argues their long life in belief comes from possession of a living host, not from a corpse walking. Phi krasue is always female in her account. Phi pop is often thought shapeless and can possess men or women. Regional names overlap, and in some places phi pop, phi krasue, and phi thamop are distinct.

sources.title: Pop (ghost)
sources.supports: Cannibalistic viscera-eating spirit, related to Phi Fa.

sources.title: Katarzyna Ancuta, Beyond the Vampire, eTropic 16.1 (2017)
sources.supports: Viscera appetite; living belief; possession rather than a walking corpse; pop can be shapeless and of either sex.

parodyPotential: A possession that makes the host hungry for the wrong pantry. Living belief, and not a prop for mocking rural people. Phi Fa is only a name here.

name: Phi Tai Hong (ผีตายโหง)
facts: Phi Tai Hong is a ghost of Thai folklore: the vengeful, restless spirit of a person who died suddenly by violence or cruelty.

sources.title: Phi Tai Hong
sources.supports: Restless ghost of a sudden violent or cruel death.

parodyPotential: A restless death, not a slapstick corpse. If used, the joke cannot be the death itself.

name: Kuman thong (กุมารทอง)
facts: A kuman thong is a household deity of Thai folk religion, believed to bring luck, fortune, and wealth if properly revered. Kuman, from Pali kumara, means young boy; thong means golden.
The English lead says these beings are often worshipped so they will obey requests for gain, protection, wealth, and in some cases harm, and that each request is believed to have consequences.
The lead that was read does not describe how such a figure is made. No ritual claim is added.

sources.title: Kuman thong
sources.supports: Household boy-deity of luck; requests are believed to carry consequences.

parodyPotential: Do not make a card. This is a living child-spirit practice.

name: Nang Kwak (นางกวัก)
facts: Nang Kwak is a bodhisattva, household goddess, or spirit of Thai folklore, believed to bring fortune, prosperity, and customers.

The article says she is more a figure of popular folklore than a deity, while Buddhist legends try to fold her into Buddhism. She is commonly dressed in red Thai clothing, called an incarnation of Mae Po Sop the rice goddess, and compared with Lakshmi.
She is found among shops and merchants.

sources.title: Nang Kwak
sources.supports: Shop spirit in red who beckons customers; linked to the rice goddess.

parodyPotential: Do not make her a monster. She is a living shop blessing, tied to the rice goddess.

name: Nariphon
facts: The Himavanta article says the mythical Nariphon tree, often mentioned in Thai folklore, grows in the Himavanta forest.
The lead does not describe the tree's fruit or any maiden-shaped crop. That detail is not claimed from this page.

sources.title: Himavanta
sources.supports: Names the Nariphon as a mythical tree of Thai folklore growing in Himavanta.

parodyPotential: A named mythical tree and nothing more until a page that describes it is fetched.

name: Phaya Nak / Nāga
origin: Hindu and Buddhist tradition; Thai Himmaphan literature
facts: English Wikipedia redirects Phaya Naga to Nāga. Nāgas are a divine or semi-divine race of half-human, half-serpent beings in Asian religious traditions, living in Patala, also known as dragons and water spirits. A female is a nagini. Rituals for them have been held in South Asia for at least two thousand years.
They are shown as humans with snakes on the head and neck, as serpents, or as half-human half-snake beings in Hindu and Buddhist art. Nagaraja is the title of a naga king.
The Thai Traibhumikatha tradition of Himavanta, as summarized in English, places Phaya Naga among the beings of that forest, with Phaya Krut and Kinnaree.

sources.title: Nāga
sources.supports: Divine or semi-divine serpent race; Phaya Naga redirects here; long ritual history.

sources.title: Himavanta
sources.supports: Thai literary forest that houses Phaya Naga, Phaya Krut, and Kinnaree.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Naga are worshipped, and Phaya Nak is a sacred Himmaphan and Mekong being, not a boss gag.

name: Garuda / Phaya Krut (ครุฑ)
origin: Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain tradition; Thai and Indonesian state insignia
facts: Garuda is a Hindu deity, primarily the mount of Vishnu, and is also present in Buddhist and Jain tradition. He is king of birds, shown as a giant kite-like bird or as a winged man, a protector and an enemy of serpents.
He is part of the state insignia of India, Indonesia, and Thailand.
The Himavanta article names Phaya Krut among the creatures of that Thai literary forest, beside Phaya Naga and Kinnaree.

sources.title: Garuda
sources.supports: Vishnu's mount; king of birds; state insignia of India, Indonesia, and Thailand.

sources.title: Himavanta
sources.supports: Phaya Krut is named in the Thai Himavanta forest.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Garuda is a deity and a national emblem.

name: Kinnara / Kinnaree (กินรี)
origin: Hindu and Buddhist mythology; Thai Himmaphan literature
facts: A kinnara is a Hindu and Buddhist being, part human and part bird, strongly tied to music and love, believed to come from the Himalayas and to watch over humans in trouble.
In the Mahabharata's Adi Parva they describe themselves as eternal lovers who never separate and never become parents.
In Southeast Asian Buddhist art, kinnaris, the women, are half-bird, half-woman. The Himavanta article names Kinnaree among the forest's beings.

sources.title: Kinnara
sources.supports: Half-human half-bird musicians and lovers; Southeast Asian kinnari are half-bird women.

sources.title: Himavanta
sources.supports: Kinnaree is named in the Thai Himavanta forest.

parodyPotential: A heavenly musician, not a monster punchline. Sacred Buddhist and Hindu art.

name: Pret / Preta
origin: Buddhist, Hindu, and Thai ghost belief
facts: Preta, often translated hungry ghost, is a being in Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, and Chinese folk religion who suffers more than humans, especially from extreme hunger and thirst.
Early sources such as the Petavatthu are more varied than the later hungry-ghost picture. Passing on is tied to rites and offerings by the family.
The English article on ghosts in Thai culture says Thai belief mixes Buddhist popular ideas with local spirits, and names the tall preta as one figure that comes from Buddhist mythology.

sources.title: Preta
sources.supports: Hungry ghost of extreme hunger and thirst across Hindu, Buddhist, and Chinese tradition.

sources.title: Ghosts in Thai culture
sources.supports: The tall preta is part of Thai ghost lore via Buddhism.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. The pret is a religious image of suffering and craving, still part of merit-making.

name: Himavanta (หิมพานต์)
facts: Himavanta, also called Himmapan or Himmapun Mountain, is a legendary forest said to lie in the Himalayas.
It appears in the Thai Traibhumikatha, which places there many mythical creatures, including Phaya Naga, Phaya Krut, and Kinnaree, plus spirits and gods. The Nariphon tree is also said to grow there.

The account of the three planes and this forest is credited to Phaya Lithai of Si Satchanalai. Because the forest belongs to Buddhist cosmology, it shapes belief, culture, and art in Buddhist and Hindu settings.

sources.title: Himavanta
sources.supports: Legendary forest in Traibhumikatha; home of Phaya Naga, Phaya Krut, Kinnaree, and the Nariphon.

parodyPotential: A tower environment, not a single enemy, and not a joke about Buddhist cosmology.

name: Chao phi (เจ้าผี)
facts: Phya Anuman Rajadhon writes that Thai phi once covered both gods and devils. After Thai contact with Hinduized Khmer culture, good phi were renamed thevada, from Sanskrit deva, and phi narrowed toward ghost, devil, or evil spirit, though the older sense survives in some phrases.

Chao phi, a lord or prince phi, sit on the border between gods and devils and are sometimes also called thevada. Each desolate place has a chao phi over its lesser phi. People build a shrine and make offerings. The chao phi is a tutelary spirit, arak or theparak. Worshippers address the lord father or lord mother and call themselves an elephant calf.

sources.title: Phya Anuman Rajadhon, The Phi (Journal of the Siam Society, 1954 PDF)
sources.supports: Phi once included gods; chao phi are shrine guardians on the border of thevada.

parodyPotential: Do not make a boss. Chao phi are guardians with shrines. Not every phi is a monster.

name: Yaksha (ยักษ์ / yakkha)
origin: Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist tradition, including Southeast Asian temples
facts: Yakshas are a broad class of nature spirits in Hindu mythology, tied to water, trees, forests, wilderness, treasure, and fertility. They are usually benevolent and sometimes mischievous. A feminine form is the yakshi.
They appear in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist texts and as guardian deities on ancient and medieval temples in South and Southeast Asia.
The same article gives them a second face: an inoffensive wood and mountain spirit, or a darker ghost that haunts the wild and devours travelers, compared there with rakshasas.

sources.title: Yaksha
sources.supports: Nature spirits and temple guardians; a darker traveler-devouring version is also described.

parodyPotential: Temple guardians are sacred. A wild, traveler-waylaying yaksha is the only version that could become an enemy, and even then not as a mockery of temple statues.

name: Aswang
facts: Aswang is a general term for evil shapeshifting creatures in Filipino folklore: vampires, ghouls, witches, viscera suckers, and human-beast hybrids, usually dogs, cats, or pigs.

Spanish colonists in the 16th century already recorded the aswang as the most feared mythical creature in the islands. The article reads their behavior as an inversion of traditional Filipino values, without a motive beyond harm.
The tradition is especially popular in southern Luzon, parts of Mindanao, and the Visayas, notably Capiz. Manananggal is a separate, more specific creature and should not be the same card.

sources.title: Aswang
sources.supports: Umbrella term for shapeshifting evil beings; feared in Spanish-era reports; Capiz and other regions.

parodyPotential: A category boss only if the card is clearly a shapeshifter-of-the-week, not a copy of one subtype.

name: Manananggal
facts: Manananggal, literally 'remover', is a Philippine mythical creature that can split its upper torso from the lower body. Fangs and wings give it a vampire-like look.
The krasue article calls the manananggal a Philippine spirit that haunts pregnant women and distinguishes it from head-only flying spirits because the lower half of the body detaches.

sources.title: Manananggal
sources.supports: Separates the upper torso; fangs and wings.

sources.title: Krasue
sources.supports: Groups the manananggal as the Philippine form that haunts pregnant women and splits at the waist.

parodyPotential: A self-separating flyer. Do not build the joke on hunting pregnant women. Not a krasue with a new hat.

name: Tikbalang
facts: The tikbalang is a Philippine folklore creature of mountains and rainforests: a tall bony humanoid with a horse's head and hooves, and limbs so long that its knees reach above its head when it squats.
In some versions it is a transformation of an aborted fetus sent from limbo. That is one version in the article, not the only one.

sources.title: Tikbalang
sources.supports: Horse-headed, long-limbed mountain humanoid; one version links it to an aborted fetus.

parodyPotential: Use the backwards-looking horse giant and the impossible squat. Do not use the fetus version.

name: Kapre
facts: A kapre is a human-like mythical creature described as a tree giant: tall, dark, hairy, and muscular.
In Philippine folklore, kapre sit in fruitless trees, smoke large cigars, and are mischievous but benign toward nearby travelers.

sources.title: Kapre
sources.supports: Hairy tree giant with a large cigar; mischievous and mostly benign.

parodyPotential: A tree landlord whose cigar is bigger than the party and whose mischief stops short of murder.

name: Tiyanak
facts: The tiyanak is a vampiric Philippine creature that takes the form of a toddler or a newborn. It cries in the jungle to draw travelers, then reverts and attacks when it is picked up.
It is also said to enjoy leading travelers astray or abducting children.

sources.title: Tiyanak
sources.supports: Baby-form vampire that cries to be picked up, then attacks.

parodyPotential: Do not make a comedy card about a crying baby that attacks. The record exists so the idea is not stumbled into.

name: Nuno sa punso
facts: A nuno sa punso, 'old man of the mound', is a dwarf-like nature spirit believed to live in an anthill or termite mound. Nuno means old man, grandparent, or ancestor.

sources.title: Nuno sa punso
sources.supports: Dwarf ancestor spirit living in an anthill.

parodyPotential: A tiny landlord of a dirt mound. The custom of asking permission is respect, not the punchline.

name: Bakunawa
facts: The Bakunawa is a dragon-like serpent in Philippine mythology that causes natural events, above all eclipses. It is called the moon-eating dragon. Its movements were a geomantic calendar and part of babaylan ritual.
It is usually drawn with a looped tail and one horn on the nose, and was thought to live in the sky or the underworld.
Later trade and Indianization syncretized it with the naga, Rahu, and Ketu.

sources.title: Bakunawa
sources.supports: Moon-eating serpent; eclipse; babaylan calendar; later tied to naga, Rahu, and Ketu.

parodyPotential: A moon-eater whose horn and looped tail are the silhouette. Babaylan ritual and the Hindu identification are not the joke.

name: Bungisngis
facts: Bungisngis is a one-eyed giant of Philippine folklore, said to live at Meluz, Orion in Bataan, and in Batangas, and described as always laughing. The name is tied to the Cebuano ngisi, to giggle.

It shows large teeth, an upper lip that can cover the face when thrown back, and two long tusks. The single eye is in the forehead. Hearing is strong, and so is the body: in 'The Three Friends' it throws a carabao so hard the animal lands knee-deep. The same tale says it is easily outwitted and panics, and the monkey's tricks lead to its death.

sources.title: Bungisngis
sources.supports: Laughing one-eyed tusked giant; strong, easily fooled, panics.

parodyPotential: A giggling one-eyed giant who can throw a buffalo and still loses to a bad plan.

name: Berberoka
facts: The Berberoka is a swamp creature of Apayao, Abra, and Ilocos Norte. It sucks the water out of a pond so the fish lie on the mud. When people come for the fish, it releases the water and eats them as they struggle.
It can also spray water like a hose until a victim drowns. Despite that power, these water ogres have a fear of crabs.

sources.title: Berberoka
sources.supports: Drains a pond as bait; fears crabs; can hose victims with the water.

parodyPotential: A pond that inhales, then panics at a crab.

name: Bal-bal
facts: A bal-bal is an undead monster that steals corpses from funerals or graves and eats them. It smells out dead bodies and has claws and teeth that can rip burial clothes. It eats only corpses, so its breath is foul.
After eating, it leaves a banana-tree trunk in the coffin so the theft is not obvious.
The article associates it with aswang, amalanhig, and busaw as flesh eaters.

sources.title: Bal-Bal
sources.supports: Corpse thief that leaves a banana trunk in the coffin.

parodyPotential: A grave robber whose alibi is a banana trunk. Dark, not a joke about a real funeral.

name: Amalanhig
facts: Amalanhig, also maranhig or amaranhig, are Visayan creatures, especially among Hiligaynon speakers. One account says they are aswang who failed to pass on their monstrosity, so they rise from the grave and kill by biting the neck.
A word-of-mouth version says they chase the living and tickle them until they die of laughter and terror.
They look human, often with enlarged upper canines. The article calls them a Philippine vampire variant.

sources.title: Amalanhig
sources.supports: Grave-rising aswang variant; neck bite or death by tickling.

parodyPotential: The tickle version is the comedy door. The neck-bite version can stay in the research note.

name: Wakwak
facts: The wakwak is a vampiric bird-like creature said to snatch people at night. Unlike the manananggal it cannot split its torso. Some call it a vampire; others, a night bird tied to witches.

It is named for the wing sound, heard only while hunting. The sound gets softer as it comes closer. Loud means far; faint means it is about to attack. Ekek is distinguished by a bird bill the wakwak lacks.

It is often given long sharp talons and bat-like wings, the wings said to be knife-sharp. The article also says the terrifying wakwak is becoming rarer as a belief and is mostly told to scare children, and that a gecko's night call has been mistaken for it.

sources.title: Wakwak
sources.supports: Night bird-vampire; the flap grows quieter as it approaches; cannot split like a manananggal.

parodyPotential: A hunter you locate by the volume going the wrong way.

name: Minokawa
facts: Minokawa is a giant dragon-like bird. Early people used it to explain eclipses: it is large enough to swallow or cover the sun. One description puts it in outer space, able to devour the sun and the moon and willing to try the earth.
In a Bagobo tale it is as large as an island. Its feathers are sharp swords, its eyes reflect like mirrors, and its beak and legs are like steel. It lives outside the sky, at the eastern horizon.

sources.title: Minokawa
sources.supports: Island-sized eclipse bird; sword feathers; steel beak and legs; eastern horizon beyond the sky.

parodyPotential: An eclipse bird so large the fight is about its shadow, not its hit points.

name: Penanggalan
facts: The penanggalan, or penanggal, is a nocturnal Malay vampire: a floating woman's head with organs and entrails, twinkling from afar like a ball of flame.

The name comes from tanggal, to remove or take off. The article says it is not a classical undead so much as a witch who gained the form by meditation in a vat of vinegar. By day, or whenever it is attached, it is a living person.

It hunts at night for menstrual blood and birth blood, and also for pregnant women and young boys. The article lists ahp, kasu, krasue, leyak, ma lai, and manananggal as regional cousins, not duplicates.

sources.title: Penanggalan
sources.supports: Vinegar-witch whose head detaches; flame-like glow; living by day.

parodyPotential: The daytime person and the vinegar vat are the card. Do not make a mechanic out of hunting women in childbirth or boys.

name: Kuntilanak / Pontianak
facts: Kuntilanak is the Indonesian name, and pontianak the Malay name, for a vengeful spirit in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. She usually looks like a beautiful woman and shows an ugly monstrous form if she must.
One account says she is the stillborn child of a langsuir. Another calls her an angry female spirit, or the ghost or white lady of Southeast Asian folklore.
She is often a long-haired woman in white who lures men. Signs of her nearness are a baby crying and the smell of a corpse or of plumeria.

sources.title: Kuntilanak
sources.supports: Vengeful woman in white; baby cry and plumeria or decay; langsuir-child is only one origin.

parodyPotential: A white-dressed voice that smells of frangipani. Do not punch down at death in childbirth. The city of Pontianak is not this spirit.

name: Pocong
facts: A pocong is a ghost that looks like a body wrapped in a shroud. In Islamic funerals the kain kafan is tied over the head, under the feet, and around the neck.
The belief is that the knots must be undone in the grave. If they are not, the corpse animates and is called a pocong. In Malaysia the same ghost is Hantu Bungkus, the wrapped-up ghost.

sources.title: Pocong
sources.supports: Shroud-wrapped ghost caused by burial knots left tied; Malay name hantu bungkus.

parodyPotential: A wrapped figure who cannot walk until someone unties the knots. Do not mock Islamic burial. The hop is the tied feet, not a jiangshi copy.

name: Leyak
facts: The leyak is a Balinese mythological figure: a flying head with entrails, including heart, lung, and liver, still attached.
Leyak are said to fly in search of a pregnant woman, to suck her baby's blood, or of a newborn child.
Rangda is the demon queen of the leyaks in a separate article. That sacred figure is not this record's comedy target.

sources.title: Leyak
sources.supports: Balinese flying head with entrails, seeking a pregnant woman or a newborn.

parodyPotential: Do not build a card on attacking a newborn. Rangda's dance is sacred and is filed separately.

name: Pelesit
facts: Pelesit is a familiar spirit in Malay folklore, generally a cricket, sometimes a grasshopper. The name means buzzer, from lesit.

The article also says they are called palasik. Belief is traced to Malay animism before monotheism. A pelesit can only be owned by a woman in the general account, and the belief was said to be prevalent in Kedah. The male counterpart is the bajang. The two are sometimes confused.
The krasue and penanggalan articles use pelasik or pelesit in lists of flying-head spirits. That conflicts with the cricket description. Both statements are reported; they are not reconciled here.

sources.title: Pelesit
sources.supports: Cricket or grasshopper familiar; woman owner; Kedah; male pair is the bajang; also called palasik on this page.

sources.title: Penanggalan
sources.supports: Lists pelasik and pelesit among flying-head names, which disagrees with the cricket article.

parodyPotential: A cricket familiar. Do not merge it with a flying head until the name clash is checked. Confidence is medium because the sources disagree.

name: Hantu Raya
facts: Hantu Raya, roughly 'great ghost', is a familiar spirit that acts as a double for a black-magic practitioner and is supposed to give its master great power.
Folktale form: a humanoid with a black hairy body except the face, rough grey skin, long sharp teeth, and red eyes.

sources.title: Hantu Raya
sources.supports: Familiar double; hairy black body, grey skin, sharp teeth, red eyes.

parodyPotential: A stunt double who shows up when the caster is supposed to be elsewhere.

name: Sundel bolong
facts: A sundel bolong is an Indonesian ghost, a woman with long black hair and a long white dress, similar in outline to the pontianak.
The myth is closely linked to prostitutes. The name is explained as a prostitute with a hole, referring to a large hole said to appear in her back.

sources.title: Sundel bolong
sources.supports: White-dressed woman with a hole in her back; the name is tied to prostitution.

parodyPotential: The visual is a back that is a window. Do not make the joke about sex workers.

name: Wewe Gombel
facts: Wewe Gombel is a female supernatural being or vengeful ghost in Javanese mythology, said to kidnap children.
The myth is taught so children stay home at night. She is traditionally a woman with long hanging breasts. Modern pictures add vampire fangs. She also appears in comics.

sources.title: Wewe Gombel
sources.supports: Child-snatching ghost; long breasts; a cautionary night story.

parodyPotential: A night curfew story. Do not make child-snatching the fun part. Fangs are a modern add.

name: Orang bunian
origin: Malay, Singaporean, Bruneian, and Indonesian folklore
facts: Orang bunian, literally hidden people or whistling people, are supernatural beings invisible to most humans, except those with spiritual sight. English often translates them as elves.
They are described as beautiful, dressed in an old Southeast Asian style, and nearly identical to humans. Some accounts say they lack a philtrum.
Modern pictures that add pointed ears, high-fantasy clothes, or a modern Minangkabau coat depart from the traditional description.

sources.title: Orang bunian
sources.supports: Invisible beautiful hidden people; sometimes no philtrum; elf ears are a modern change.

parodyPotential: Neighbors who are present and uninvited to be photographed. Not a demon.

name: Toyol / tuyul
facts: A toyol or tuyul is an undead infant in Indonesian and Malay folklore, also found in other Southeast Asian mythologies. Shamans (dukun, pawang, or bomoh) invoke it by black magic as a helper.
A common use is theft for the owner's gain, compared in the article to the boar demon babi ngepet and the familiar hantu raya. It is said to bring luck to its host and mishap to everyone else.

sources.title: Toyol
sources.supports: Undead infant familiar used for theft; invoked by a shaman.

parodyPotential: Do not make a card. This is a child-spirit practice.

name: Ahp (អាប)
facts: The krasue article names Ahp (Khmer អាប) as the Cambodian member of the flying-head group: a woman, half spirit and half mortal, whose head and organs leave the body at night.

Ethnologist Ang Choulean, reported by Cambodianess from a 2022 talk at the Royal University of Fine Arts, describes the ahp, which he also calls krasue, as an ordinary village person by day: lazy, unwashed, avoiding farm work, asking door to door for vegetables and spices. At night or in the rain the head leaves, intestines glowing, and flies low for food. He says the favored food is the blood of a woman who has just given birth. The English report uses 'his' for this being.

sources.title: Krasue
sources.supports: Names the Khmer ahp as the Cambodian flying head with organs.

sources.title: Cambodianess, Ethnologist Ang Choulean on Cambodian spirits (20 March 2022)
sources.supports: Daytime ordinary beggar of spices; nighttime glowing entrails; birth-blood as the desired food.

parodyPotential: The daytime spice-borrower is the distinctive note. Do not make a card about blood from childbirth. Not a relabel of the Thai krasue.

name: Ngeuak
facts: A Luang Prabang culture page, drawing on Mayoury and Pheuiphanh Ngaosrivathana and on Archaimbault, says naga and ngeuak are both water spirits of rivers, ponds, and the underground.
Naga are generally benevolent guardians if shown respect. Ngeuak may be malevolent, are often associated with drownings, and must be propitiated.
The page treats named guardian naga of the city as sacred. This record is only the ngeuak as the dangerous counterpart, not those named guardians and not the 1931 royal drowning.

sources.title: Nagas and Ngeuak, Luang Prabang Culture
sources.supports: Ngeuak are water spirits, unlike benevolent naga, linked to drownings and offerings.

parodyPotential: A river serpent that is explicitly not the temple naga. Still propitiated: no joke about drownings or about Luang Prabang's guardian rites. Confidence is medium because this is a secondary site.

name: Neak ta (អ្នកតា)
facts: A neak ta is a Cambodian ancestral or tutelary deity, believed to watch over people, places, and things if they are paid proper respect.
The name translates as the ancestor. A neak ta can be feminine or masculine, and they most often work as a couple.

sources.title: Neak ta
sources.supports: Ancestral tutelary deity, often a couple, who protects what is respected.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Neak ta are living tutelary deities.

name: Rangda
facts: Rangda is the demon queen of the leyaks in traditional Balinese mythology. She is terrifying and is described as child-eating. She leads evil witches against Barong, leader of the forces of good.
Their battle is danced as the eternal fight of good and evil. Rangda is an Old Javanese word meaning widow.

sources.title: Rangda
sources.supports: Demon queen of leyaks; ritual dance against Barong; name means widow.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Rangda is a sacred dance figure, not a horror mascot.

name: Barong
facts: Barong, a word glossed as bear, is a panther-like creature and character in Balinese culture. He is king of the spirits, leader of the hosts of good, and enemy of Rangda.
The Barong dance stages their battle as the eternal fight of good and evil.

sources.title: Barong (mythology)
sources.supports: Panther-like king of good spirits; ritual opponent of Rangda.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Barong is a sacred protector in living dance.

name: Nyi Roro Kidul
facts: Nyi Roro Kidul, also Nyai Rara Kidul, is a supernatural being in Indonesian folklore, Queen of the Southern Sea in Sundanese and Javanese mythology.

One Javanese account ties Kanjeng Ratu Kidul to a creation of Dewa Kaping Telu and to harvest and nature, and says Nyi Roro Kidul was a daughter of the king of Sunda, expelled because of her stepmother.
