Some people equate the two queens; Kejawen belief, as the article states it, makes Nyi Roro Kidul a loyal subordinate of Kanjeng Ratu Kidul.
Her place as the Phantom Queen of Java is a popular motif and is tied to the beauty of Sundanese princesses.

sources.title: Nyai Roro Kidul
sources.supports: Queen of the Southern Sea; identity with Kanjeng Ratu Kidul is disputed in the article.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. She is a sea queen of living Javanese and Sundanese belief.

name: Vietnamese dragon (rồng)
facts: Vietnamese dragons are symbolic creatures of Vietnamese folklore and mythology. An origin myth says the Vietnamese people descend from a dragon and an immortal.

The dragon stands for rain, which agriculture needs, and for the emperor, prosperity, and the power of the nation. Like the Chinese dragon that influenced it, it is a fierce but benevolent serpent and a symbol of yang, the universe, life, and growth.

sources.title: Vietnamese dragon
sources.supports: National rain and sovereignty symbol; descent from a dragon and an immortal.

parodyPotential: Do not parody the origin myth or the national symbol.

name: Sơn Tinh and Thủy Tinh
facts: Sơn Tinh – Thủy Tinh, the mountain god against the lord of the waters, is a Vietnamese myth that explains tidal irrigation and monsoon floods.
Sơn Tinh is also one of the Four Immortals, specifically Tản Viên Sơn Thánh.

sources.title: Sơn Tinh – Thủy Tinh
sources.supports: Mountain god versus water lord as the myth of floods; Son Tinh is a Four Immortal.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Sơn Tinh is one of the Four Immortals. The flood rivalry can be noted as myth, not as a comedy boss.

name: Nghê
facts: Nghê is a mythical animal in Vietnamese culture, a combination of lion and dog, often used as a mascot in front of communal temples, temples, pagodas, and shrines.

sources.title: Nghê
sources.supports: Lion-dog guardian figure at Vietnamese temples and shrines.

parodyPotential: A threshold lion-dog. Temple guardians are not enemies.

name: Hamsa (หงส์)
facts: The hamsa is an aquatic migratory bird in ancient Sanskrit texts. Scholars have read the image as goose, swan, or flamingo.
In Indian and Southeast Asian culture it is a spiritual symbol and a decoration. Myth gives it the power to separate milk from water, or good from evil.
In Hindu iconography the hamsa is the vahana of Brahma, Gayatri, Saraswati, and Vishvakarma. This page does not itself equate the bird with the Lao town Hongsa or spell the Thai name.

sources.title: Hamsa (bird)
sources.supports: Sacred aquatic bird; separates milk from water; vehicle of Brahma and Saraswati.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. The hamsa is a sacred vehicle and symbol.

name: Makara
facts: Makara is a legendary sea creature in Hindu mythology and, in Hindu astrology, the sign Capricorn.

It is the vahana of the river goddesses Ganga and Narmada and of Varuna, god of the ocean. Makara guard gateways and thresholds, including throne rooms and temple entries, and are among the most common creatures in Hindu and Buddhist temple art. They also appear as gargoyles or as spouts on springs.

sources.title: Makara
sources.supports: Sea creature; vehicle of Ganga and Varuna; temple threshold guardian.

parodyPotential: Do not parody. Makara are temple guardians and vehicles of gods.

name: Sarimanok
facts: The sarimanok, feminine form papanok, is a legendary bird of the Maranao people of Mindanao.

The name joins sari, assorted or various, and manok, which early Spanish sources used for bird and which later narrowed to chicken. The article glosses the creature as a bird, or chicken, of assorted colors.
The lead does not describe a fish in the talons or a luck charm. Those details are not added.

sources.title: Sarimanok
sources.supports: Maranao legendary bird; name means a bird of assorted colors.

parodyPotential: A many-colored bird and a Maranao symbol. Do not turn the name into a chicken joke.

name: Siyokoy
facts: A siyokoy is an aquatic humanoid in Philippine mythology, often described with scales, webbed limbs, and fins.
Most legends make siyokoy hostile to humans, and they are said to drown people.

sources.title: Siyokoy
sources.supports: Scaled, webbed, finned humanoid that drowns people.

parodyPotential: A scaled swimmer of the tower cistern, distinct from a mermaid and from a naga.

name: Mandurugo
facts: The mandurugo is a kind of aswang, similar to a vampire, in stories popular among Tagalog and Bicol speakers. There are many variations.
By day they are usually young beautiful women. By night they grow wings and a long sharp tongue, used to cut a man's neck or to prick the inside of his mouth while kissing, to take blood.
Sometimes the mandurugo marries an unsuspecting man as cover and flies to other villages to feed.

sources.title: Mandurugo
sources.supports: Daytime woman, nighttime wings and tongue; blood taken by a cut or a kiss.

parodyPotential: A day-face and a night-tongue. Keep it separate from manananggal, which splits at the waist.

name: Polong
facts: The polong is a familiar spirit in Malay folklore, a miniature woman the size of the first joint of a finger.
It is one of the ghosts named in Hikayat Abdullah, by Abdullah bin Abdul Kadir.
The penanggalan article separately mentions a 'hantu polong' of the Temuan in a flying-head list. That may be a different use of the word. This record follows the finger-sized familiar.

sources.title: Polong
sources.supports: Finger-sized woman familiar, named in Hikayat Abdullah.

parodyPotential: A familiar small enough to hide in a thimble. Do not merge her with the flying head without a source that does so on purpose.

name: Hitodama (人魂)
facts: Hitodama, 'human soul', are balls of fire that float in the night air. They are also called onibi, demon fires, or hikarimono, glowing things.
They are said to be souls of the dead that have separated from their bodies, which is where the name comes from.

sources.title: Hitodama
sources.supports: Night fireballs that are separated souls of the dead.

parodyPotential: A lost soul that is only a light, useful as a telegraph, not as a boss.

name: Yamauba (山姥)
facts: Yamauba, also yamamba and yamanba, is a yōkai mostly said to resemble a woman. She may be shown as a predatory monster or as a benevolent being.
The oni article says female oni are sometimes called yamauba.

sources.title: Yama-uba
sources.supports: Mountain woman yokai, predatory or kind depending on the telling.

sources.title: Oni
sources.supports: Female oni are sometimes called yamauba.

parodyPotential: A mountain host who might feed the party or be the meal. The lead does not specify a second mouth or a spinning hut.

name: Ningyo (人魚)
facts: Ningyo, 'human fish', is a being with both human and fish features in Japanese literature. The word is not gender-specific and covers what English calls mermaids and mermen.
The lead that was read does not say that eating the flesh grants long life, or that a ningyo's prophecy must be heeded. Those points are not claimed here.

sources.title: Ningyo
sources.supports: Human-fish, not specifically female; further powers not in the lead.

parodyPotential: A human-fish who corrects anyone who calls them a mermaid. Do not add the immortality meal without a fetched page.

name: Dodomeki (百々目鬼)
facts: A dodomeki, also todomeki, is a yōkai depicted as a woman cursed with long arms covered in hundreds of bird eyes because she stole money.

sources.title: Dodomeki
sources.supports: Thief cursed with eye-covered long arms.

parodyPotential: A pickpocket whose arms grew eyes and can no longer work unnoticed.

name: Jubokko (樹木子)
origin: Japanese folklore, as presented in yokai books
facts: The English article calls the jubokko a yōkai tree that appears in many yokai books, including Shigeru Mizuki's works.

According to the folklore as that article states it, the tree stands on an old battlefield, looks ordinary, and became a yokai by drinking the blood of the dead. It catches passersby, turns branches into tubes, and drinks their blood, which keeps it looking fresh. Cut it, and blood runs. A branch is said to be able to heal and cleanse a wound.
The lead does not cite a premodern collection. Confidence stays medium.

sources.title: Jubokko
sources.supports: Battlefield blood tree in yokai books; healing branch; antiquity not shown in the lead.

parodyPotential: A pretty tree on a battlefield that is too green. Do not present it as ancient if the only cite is modern yokai books.

name: Funayūrei (船幽霊)
facts: Funayūrei, 'boat spirits', are yūrei who became vengeful ghosts at sea. Stories are told in many regions, in Edo ghost tales and in modern folk custom.
In Yamaguchi and Saga they are called ayakashi.
The lead does not give the ladle trick. That trick is sourced for umibozu, not for this ghost.

sources.title: Funayūrei
sources.supports: Vengeful ghosts of the sea; called ayakashi in Yamaguchi and Saga.

parodyPotential: A drowned crew that wants the boat stopped. Do not copy the umibozu's bottomless ladle onto them.

name: Nure-onna (濡女)
facts: Nure-onna, 'wet woman', is a yōkai with a woman's head and a snake's body. At sea the same phenomenon is called nureyomejo.
Legends often say they eat humans, but the article says they have no single appearance or personality.

sources.title: Nure-onna
sources.supports: Snake-bodied woman of the shore or sea; personality is not fixed.

parodyPotential: A shore serpent whose mood is not in the manual. Do not lock one tale's baby-bundle trick; it was not in the lead.

name: Ushi-oni (牛鬼)
facts: The ushi-oni, or gyūki, is a yōkai of western Japan. More than one kind exists, but a bovine head is the common picture.
They generally appear on beaches and attack people walking there.

sources.title: Ushi-oni
sources.supports: Ox-headed beach monster of western Japan; several local kinds.

parodyPotential: A beach ox-demon. Spider-bodied variants were not in the lead and are not claimed.

name: Inugami (犬神)
facts: Inugami, 'dog god' or 'dog spirit', is spiritual possession by a dog, widely known in western Japan, with a strong footing into recent years in eastern Oita, Shimane, and part of Kochi. A theory in the article makes Shikoku, where foxes were absent, the main home of the belief.
Traces are also described in Yamaguchi, Kyushu, the Satsunan islands, and Okinawa. Local pronunciations include ingami and irigami.
The lead describes the geography of the belief. It does not describe a ritual for making an inugami. No such ritual is added.

sources.title: Inugami
sources.supports: Dog-spirit possession, especially western Japan and Shikoku; creation ritual not in the lead.

parodyPotential: A dog spirit that possesses, not a pet. Do not invent the cruel making-ritual from memory.

name: Tōfu-kozō (豆腐小僧)
facts: Tōfu-kozō, 'tofu boy', is a yōkai that looks like a child carrying a tray of tofu.

He is frequent in Edo kusazōshi, kibyōshi, and kaidan, and from the Bakumatsu into Meiji he was a familiar character on toys: kites, sugoroku, and karuta. He also shows up in senryū, kyōka, theater pamphlets, and nishiki-e.

sources.title: Tōfu-kozō
sources.supports: Child yokai with a tofu tray; an Edo print and toy character.

parodyPotential: A delivery boy who will not put the tray down. He is a print character, not a child-spirit cult.

name: Aoandon (青行燈)
facts: Aoandon, 'blue andon', is a creature Toriyama Sekien drew in Konjaku hyakki shūi to be the spirit that appears in the game of a hundred candles, hyakumonogatari kaidankai, after the last story.
The candles were often set in blue-paper andon lamps, which gives the name.
Sekien shows a woman with a blue face, two horns on the brow, and sharp teeth.

sources.title: Aoandon
sources.supports: Sekien's spirit of the last story in the hundred-candle game; blue face and horns.

parodyPotential: The thing that shows up when the party tells one story too many.

name: Mikoshi-nyūdō (見越し入道)
facts: Mikoshi-nyūdō is a bald yōkai with a neck that keeps extending. In folklore and Edo kaidan he frightens people who look over the top of a folding screen or similar barrier.
The name joins 'looking over the top' and nyūdō, a Buddhist priest or a tonsured monster.

sources.title: Mikoshi-nyūdō
sources.supports: Bald extending-neck yokai that appears when you peer over a screen.

parodyPotential: A bald head that grows to meet whoever peeks over the wall.

name: Kasha (火車)
facts: The kasha is a yōkai said to steal corpses. The name is written as fire-cart or changed-wheel.
It is now generally thought of as a cat-shaped monster, though earlier types were more demonic.

sources.title: Kasha (folklore)
sources.supports: Corpse-stealing yokai; now usually a cat; older forms more demonic.

parodyPotential: A funeral cat. The cart of fire is the name; the modern shape is the cat. Do not make a joke of a real funeral.
